_doc: Per-lesson end-of-lesson quizzes for starter courses. Keys are '<courseSlug>/<lessonIndex>' (0-based). Generated by scripts/generate-quizzes.ts from the lesson's own block content. loadCourseSeed merges these in when a lesson seed does not already declare its own .quiz. Idempotent: re-running the generator overwrites entries here, then force-reseed via /api/cron/seed-starter-courses?force=all republishes courses as a new CourseVersion.

questions.promptMd: A colleague exports a list of Client A's user mailboxes to a CSV, finishes the task, and then pastes the file into a shared {{company_name}} company-wide Teams channel so another engineer can reference it later. Which rule from the lesson does this **most directly** violate?

choices.label: Client data must never be exported to CSV format under any circumstances.
Client A's data must not sit in {{company_name}}'s general-purpose spaces where it isn't scoped to the engagement.
Technical data may only be shared with the client, never internally.
Mailbox lists are PII and therefore require encryption before any sharing.

questions.promptMd: You are wrapping up an engagement for Client B. Which of the following items **count as client data** under the lesson's working definition and therefore must be handled accordingly?

choices.label: A network diagram you drew during the engagement to map Client B's infrastructure.
A {{company_name}} internal policy document you referenced while planning the engagement.
A screenshot of Client B's tenant configuration you pasted into a chat message to explain an issue.
A CSV of Client B's mailboxes you exported temporarily to verify a count.
The fact that Client B is currently migrating off a specific platform.

questions.promptMd: Sharing an anonymised observation — such as 'one of our healthcare clients had a ransomware incident last month' without naming the client — does **not** constitute a data leak because no personally identifiable information was disclosed.

You are building a deliverable for Client B and realise that a network architecture pattern you documented for Client A would save significant time if reused. The two clients are in completely different industries and will never interact. According to the lesson, what should you do?

choices.label: Reuse the document freely, since the clients are in different industries and there is no competitive conflict.
Reuse only the non-technical sections, as business confidential data is the only category restricted from reuse.
Do not reuse Client A's data in a deliverable for Client B, regardless of industry or perceived harmlessness.
Obtain verbal approval from your manager, then reuse the document with Client A's name redacted.

questions.promptMd: Explain the distinction the lesson draws between **the four data buckets** and **metadata about the data**, and describe why metadata is treated as equally sensitive rather than as a lower-risk category.
questions.rubricMd: Must mention: (1) the four buckets are PII, business confidential, technical, and metadata about the data; (2) metadata includes facts such as which products a client uses, migration plans, or incident history — not just raw data records; (3) the lesson explicitly states metadata is data and that revealing it (even without naming the client) constitutes a leak; (4) an example illustrating how a seemingly vague metadata disclosure can still expose confidential client information.

questions.promptMd: You built a Terraform module for Client A that automates multi-region failover. Client B has an almost identical infrastructure need. What is the **correct** course of action according to {{company_name}} policy?

choices.label: Use the module directly since you wrote it and it is a {{company_name}} asset by default.
Rename the module's variables and remove Client A's account IDs, then proceed without further approval.
Either obtain explicit written approval from Client A, or extract a genuinely generic version with no client-specific content and confirm it is clean with your engagement lead.
Ask Client B to sign an NDA covering Client A's work product before sharing the module.

questions.promptMd: Sharing a high-level, abstracted pattern — such as 'here is how we typically structure a tenant migration runbook' with no client names or specifics — violates cross-client confidentiality rules under {{company_name}} policy.
During a video call with Client B, which of the following actions would constitute a **disclosure risk** under {{company_name}}'s NDA hygiene guidance? Select **all** that apply.

choices.label: Having a browser tab open with Client A's project dashboard, visible in the taskbar during screen sharing.
Mentioning that 'another customer we work with had a similar scaling issue' without naming them.
Describing the abstract pattern {{company_name}} typically uses for scaling engagements, with no client details.
Receiving a desktop notification that displays Client A's company name while your screen is shared.
Taking the call from a busy airport lounge while your screen is visible to nearby passengers.

questions.promptMd: A colleague argues: 'I stripped out Client A's name and changed a few config values — that makes the runbook generic enough to reuse for Client B without any approval.' Which statement **best** explains why this reasoning is flawed?

choices.label: It is flawed only if Client A's NDA is mutual rather than one-way.
Superficial edits do not remove the underlying problem-solving approach and competitive advantage Client A paid to build, and the contract may still assign ownership of that work product to Client A.
It is flawed because all runbooks must be rewritten from scratch for each engagement regardless of content.
It is flawed only if Client B is a direct competitor of Client A.

questions.promptMd: A consultant is about to speak at an industry conference and wants to use a real client engagement as a case study to illustrate a complex migration approach. Using the guidance from this lesson, explain the test they should apply before doing so, and describe what outcome of that test would make sharing acceptable.
questions.rubricMd: Must mention: (1) the 'conference-talk test' — asking whether the story could be told at a conference with the customer's **written permission**; (2) that sharing is acceptable only if the customer has given written permission OR the content is abstracted to a pattern with no identifying names or specifics; (3) that if names or specifics would need to be removed to make it safe, the material should remain private.

questions.promptMd: Your engagement ends on Friday. The MSA contains a **'destroy on termination'** clause with no additional conditions. You still have client data in your Downloads folder, a 1Password vault, and a GitHub repo owned by {{company_name}}. Which statement best describes your obligation?

choices.label: You must wait for the customer to formally request destruction before taking any action.
Cleanup is triggered automatically at engagement end — no customer request is needed — and must cover all locations including local files, the vault, and the repo.
Only the GitHub repo requires action; cloud-hosted data is the customer's responsibility to remove.
You have a standard 30-to-60-day window to complete cleanup regardless of which clause type the contract uses.

questions.promptMd: Which of the following practices are explicitly taught in the lesson as part of **data hygiene during an active engagement** (not just at end-of-engagement)?

choices.label: Export only the minimum number of records needed to accomplish the task at hand.
Apply the M365 retention label required by policy before the engagement closes.
Delete intermediate files such as debug logs and test CSVs once you no longer need them.
Keep the source of truth in the customer's tenant so your local copies stay minimal.
Archive the engagement vault in 1Password and rotate any shared credentials.

questions.promptMd: Retaining client data beyond what the contract requires is a defensible practice because it ensures you can respond quickly if the customer later disputes deliverables or requests historical records.

A colleague argues: *'I only need to clean up the places where I actively stored files — my laptop and GitHub. Cloud services like M365 handle their own retention automatically, so I don't need to touch them.'* Based on the lesson, what is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.label: It is correct — M365 retention policies run automatically and require no manual labelling by the consultant.

It understates the scope: cleanup must also cover 1Password vaults, customer-side guest access, personal notes apps, and any other location where data landed — and M365 requires manually applying the correct retention label, not relying on defaults.
It is partially correct; the only additional step needed is to remove guest access from the customer's M365 tenant.
It is wrong only because GitHub repos must be deleted rather than archived at engagement end.

questions.promptMd: Explain the difference between a **'return or destroy on request'** clause and a **'destroy on termination'** clause, and describe what a consultant should do if they cannot locate the relevant clause in their contract documents.
questions.rubricMd: Must mention: (1) 'return or destroy on request' requires the customer to actively ask before the obligation is triggered, typically within a 30–60 day window; (2) 'destroy on termination' triggers automatically when the engagement ends with no customer request needed; (3) if the clause cannot be found, the consultant must ask their engagement lead rather than guessing or acting unilaterally.

questions.promptMd: You accidentally emailed Client B a file containing Client A's pricing details. You realize the mistake 5 minutes later. Which action best aligns with the guidance in this lesson?

choices.label: Send a follow-up email to Client B explaining the mistake and attaching the correct file so they know which one to use.
Immediately report the incident to {{company_name}} IT or your manager via the fastest available channel, and preserve the original sent email as evidence.
Delete the sent email from your Sent folder to limit further exposure, then notify your manager once you've cleaned up.
Wait to see if Client B responds before escalating, since they may not have opened the attachment yet.

questions.promptMd: Which of the following actions are explicitly warned against in the lesson when responding to a data handling incident? **Select all that apply.**

choices.label: Deleting the wrong-recipient email or suspicious file before the response team has reviewed it.
Reporting the incident via a brief, imperfect one-liner message rather than a fully drafted explanation.
Emailing the affected client to apologize and clarify, inadvertently re-sending the exposed data in the process.
Writing down the time, recipient, and content of what was sent while the details are still fresh.
Attempting to self-remediate in a way that creates additional exposure of the original data.

questions.promptMd: According to the lesson, an employee who reports a data incident promptly is less likely to face consequences than one who conceals it, even if the underlying mistake was the same.

A colleague argues: *'I pushed a config file with a live API key to a public GitHub repo, but I deleted the repo within two minutes — so no action is needed since the exposure window was tiny.'* Based on the lesson, what is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.label: It is correct — deleting the repo within two minutes is sufficient remediation and no further steps are required.
The repo should have been made private rather than deleted, so the history is preserved for the response team.
Speed limits damage but does not eliminate the need to report; a leaked credential must be rotated by the response team, and hiding the incident risks it going uncontained.
The colleague should first verify whether the key was actually used before deciding whether to report, to avoid unnecessary escalation.

questions.promptMd: A teammate says they pasted a client's contract into a free AI tool to summarize it faster, and they're unsure whether to report it because 'nothing bad has probably happened yet.' Explain why the lesson's guidance still requires action, and describe what that action should look like.
questions.rubricMd: Must mention: (1) Speed matters — early reporting can limit or reverse damage (e.g., prompt revocation or expiry); (2) The absence of visible harm does not remove the obligation to report; (3) The correct immediate action is to notify {{company_name}} IT or a manager quickly via any available channel; (4) Evidence (e.g., the chat log or session details) should be preserved, not deleted; (5) Hiding the incident — not the mistake itself — is what creates serious risk.
